title: Too costly, compared to what?
principle: When they say "too costly", ask "compared to what?"

screens.text: Remember Nirma from Unit 1? Nirma powder cost ₹7 a kilo. Surf cost ₹28. Surf did not cut its price. Instead, in 1984, Surf's TV ads showed Lalitaji, a smart housewife who spent money carefully. She never said Surf was cheap.

screens.prompt: Surf cost four times as much as Nirma. What do you think Lalitaji said to shoppers?

options.label: Surf had a lower price this week
Surf was worth paying more for
Surf was used by rich families

screens.why: Her famous Hindi line, "Surf ki kharidari mein hi samajhdari hai", means buying Surf is a smart choice. Her point was simple: a low price does not always mean a good product. She made shoppers think about what they got for their money.

screens.title: The reference price
screens.text: Every buyer has a price they compare with. This is called the reference price. Shoppers compared Surf's ₹28 with Nirma's ₹7, so Surf seemed costly. Lalitaji made them think about what they got for the money. When a buyer says "too costly", first ask: "Compared to what?"

screens.prompt: A customer says your ₹300 haircut is "too costly". What should you ask first?

options.label: "Our barbers learned their work in Mumbai."
"What price did you expect to pay?"

screens.why: Yes. First find out what price they have in mind. If it is a ₹60 roadside haircut, you can show what is different. If it is the salon next door at ₹250, you know what they are comparing with.

wrong.a: You offered ₹50 off before asking what price they had in mind. They might have expected ₹280. First ask: "What price did you expect to pay?"
wrong.b: That may be true, but you still do not know what price they have in mind. If they expected a ₹60 roadside haircut, Mumbai training may not matter to them. Ask about the price first.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: You may face Surf's problem with your café deal too. It is March. During the two-week trial, the café owner took 10 brownies a day. They sold out most evenings. Now he wants a monthly deal, but he says ₹45 for each brownie is "too costly".

screens.prompt: His supplier's slice costs him ₹30 and sells for ₹50. Your brownie costs him ₹45 and sells for ₹80. Per brownie, he keeps…
screens.why: Yes. He keeps ₹20 on a slice (₹50 − ₹30) and ₹35 on a brownie (₹80 − ₹45). That is ₹15 more on each brownie. He was looking at what he paid, not what he kept.

wrong.a: You worked out ₹45 − ₹30. That compares what he pays. Now look at what he keeps. He gets ₹35 on a brownie (₹80 − ₹45) and ₹20 on a slice (₹50 − ₹30). That is ₹15 more.
wrong.c: Check both sums. He keeps ₹35 on a brownie (₹80 − ₹45) and ₹20 on a slice (₹50 − ₹30). So he keeps ₹15 more on a brownie.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six replies to "too costly". For each one, tell me: does it show a different comparison or cut the price?

items.text: Show what he keeps on each brownie and each slice
Take ₹5 off each brownie this month
Show how quickly your brownies sold out during the trial
Show that the chain café sells brownies for ₹70
Give him the first week free

screens.why: Good work. Some replies help him compare what he keeps, how fast the brownies sell, or a real price elsewhere. The others lower your price, so you earn less.

screens.prompt: You cut your price to ₹35 a brownie to get the deal. Later, you want ₹45 again. What problem might you face?

options.label: He thinks ₹35 is your normal price
He wants to order fewer brownies daily
He wants more days to pay you

screens.why: Right. You learned this in Unit 3: a discount can make a good product seem cheap. Once he pays ₹35, he starts to see it as your normal price. Then ₹45 feels like a price rise.

wrong.b: He may still order the same number. The problem is what he now thinks your price should be. Remember Unit 3: a discount can make a good product seem cheap. He starts to see ₹35 as your normal price.
wrong.c: Paying later is a different problem. Remember Unit 3: a discount can make a good product seem cheap. He starts to see ₹35 as your normal price.

screens.setup: It is late March. The café owner wants 70 brownies a week, as in the trial. But he says ₹45 is too costly. Each brownie costs you ₹20 to make. He sells it for ₹80. His cake slices cost him ₹30 each and sell for ₹50.
screens.question: What do you do?

options.label: Charge ₹35 per brownie, but earn less
options.outcome: He agrees at once. You earn ₹15 on each of the 70 brownies. That is ₹1,050 a week. A month later, his friend's café also asks you for ₹35.
options.why: You lowered your price to match what he expected. But he was comparing what he paid, not what he earned. Now two cafés expect you to charge ₹35.
options.better: Ask what price he compares with. Then show how much he keeps on each brownie.

options.label: Keep ₹45 per brownie, but explain its value
options.outcome: He is still unsure, so he orders 50 a week instead of 70. You earn ₹25 on each brownie. That is ₹1,250 a week.
options.why: You kept your price, which was good. But just saying your brownies are worth ₹45 is not enough. He needed to see the numbers himself.
options.better: Ask what price he compares with. Then show how much he keeps on each brownie.

options.label: Compare what he earns, but keep ₹45
options.outcome: He sees that he keeps ₹35 on a brownie but only ₹20 on a slice. "So I earn more on the costly one!" He agrees to 70 a week at ₹45. You earn ₹25 on each brownie. That is ₹1,750 a week.
options.why: You helped him compare what he earned instead of what he paid. Your price stayed the same. Now he understands why ₹45 is fair.

screens.text: When a buyer says "too costly", ask: compared to ___? Then show a fairer ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Lalitaji made shoppers think about what they got for their money, not just the price per kilo. You helped the café owner compare what he kept, not just what he paid.

summary: Reference price: the price a buyer uses to judge another price.
When a buyer says "too costly", ask "compared to what?" before you lower your price.
Show a fair comparison using real numbers: cost per use, what the buyer keeps, or a real price elsewhere.

cards.front: A buyer says your price is too high. What do you ask first?
cards.back: First find out their reference price. Then show a fairer comparison.

cards.front: A shop buys your item for ₹45 and sells it for ₹80. A rival's item costs ₹30 and sells for ₹50. Which earns more?
cards.back: Your item earns the shop ₹35. The rival's earns ₹20. Compare what the shop keeps, not just what it pays.

cards.front: Surf cost ₹28 a kilo, and Nirma cost ₹7. What did Lalitaji want shoppers to compare?
options: What they got for the money
cards.back: She wanted them to think about what they got for their money, not just the price on the packet.
